analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Thank you, counsel. The case is submitted. We'll hear arguments next in central states against central transport. Thank you. Mr. Luplo, I think you may proceed whenever you're ready now. Thank you. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the Court. This is a case of first impression, which we believe is of great national importance as it relates to the national pension policy. Petitioners of the central states' pension and health and welfare funds conduct random audits to verify whether contributing employers, such as central transport, are reporting accurately on behalf of all persons covered by applicable collective bargaining agreements. The issue in this case before this Court is whether in conducting these audits, the trustees may request access to records beyond those of employees for whom the employer admits liability. It is the trustees' claim that they have a right to a more comprehensive audit in this context under their trust agreement and under the prudent man rule of ERISA. The Sixth Circuit, in reversing the district court, limited the trustees' audit rights to records of those employees that the employer admitted were covered, and only to those unless the trustees could show cause why a particular employee was omitted, in which case that person, particular employee's records, could then be audited. The petitioners are health and welfare and pension funds located in Chicago. They're regulated by the Taft-Hartley Act and ERISA. They have over half a million participants and beneficiaries with over 12,000 employers, and there are thousands of collective bargaining agreements that apply to the fund. The Respondent Central Transport is 16 companies engaged in trucking and related industries, all parties to a collective bargaining agreement, commonly referred to as the National Master Freight Agreement, with the International Brotherhood of Teamsters. Under the collective bargaining agreement, transport obligation is to remit contributions under the collective bargaining agreement on each employee who is performing work under the collective bargaining agreement. The fund's obligations, the petitioner's obligations on the pension plan, which is related to, which is governed by the ERISA and its trust agreement, is to give credit or benefits to persons on the basis of covered employment for pensions as a matter of law if they perform work covered by the collective bargaining agreement, and this is the case regardless of whether or not the employer defaults on his contributions. The funds of necessity, because of their scope, operate on a self-reporting system, which we refer to as an honor system. The way it works simply is that the employer sends to the fund each month a list of the employees that the employer says are covered by the collective bargaining agreement, and he sends along a check for that amount. The trustees who are familiar with misreporting problems in a multi-employer setting have enacted a trust agreement that this court looked at in February of this year in Prosher and Schneider. And in that trust agreement, the trustees provided for an audit provision that provided in Article 3, Section 5, that the trustees shall be empowered to conduct on-site audits of pertinent records of a contributing employer to verify for the accuracy of the reports. And in implementing that program, the trustees conduct random audits. In this particular case, in 1980, the funds sought to conduct a random audit of Central Transport. The auditors, upon arriving or shortly thereafter at Central Transport, were told by the officials of Central Transport that 60 percent of the employees of Central Transport, which is engaged primarily in the trucking industry, were not covered by the collective bargaining agreement. The company then refused to produce any documentation to the fund's representatives to produce or to support its contention that those 60 percent of the employees were not covered. As to the records that they allowed us to audit, those of employees that they admitted they owed liability on, the fund determined that there were over $268,000 in audit findings. Now, to be sure, those audit findings are subject to the employer's... $268,000. $268,000 in audit findings, which means that a preliminary investigation by our auditors reflected that there were $268,000 in contributions that should have been sent in that were not. Well, that's all I wanted to know, what you were referring to. Okay. Thank you. Thanks. Mr. Lufflow, I take it that employees, covered employees, are required to join the union, with the union. No, they are not, Your Honor. They are not. They are definitely not. Our plan is the National Master Freight Agreement, and the plan itself does not require union membership for participation. Okay. What limits do you think ERISA may impose on the scope or frequency of audits, if your view prevails? Your Honor, I believe that the response to that has to be found in 404 of Arrested the Prudent Man Rule, and I believe that it would be what is prudent and reasonable in the circumstances. To audit an employer three or four times a year, when, in particular, prior audits indicated accurate reporting, would be unreasonable and clearly unwarranted. Is it a subject that could be covered completely by the contracts? No, Your Honor. We believe that the fiduciary duties of ERISA are the trustees alone. The union does not have a fiduciary duty. No matter what the contracts may provide you. That is correct. We are the fiduciaries exclusively under ERISA. And that would be whether the obligations under four are more or less than the contract provides? Yes, Your Honor. Well, doesn't ERISA say that the trustees shall proceed in the documents and instruments governing the plan insofar as it is not inconsistent with ERISA? Yes, that is correct, Your Honor. And you think that it would be inconsistent with ERISA for the trustees to obey a collective bargaining contract that says expressly that the employer may only and need only give a list of covered employees? That's correct. Do we have to decide that in this case? No, Your Honor. We believe that the trust agreement, in particular Article 3, Section 5, and the trust agreement, Article 4, which is the rulemaking powers of the trustees as well as their interpretive powers of the trust agreement, as incorporated by the collective bargaining agreement in Articles 55 and 56, which the transport and the union negotiated, which incorporated the trust agreement, they agreed to incorporate it, and to ratify all actions taken or to be taken by the trustees within the scope of their authority. And Article 3, Section 5 of the trust agreement is our audit authority. Well, if we agree with you, we never ever reach ERISA. I mean, we just say that as a matter of contract, the employer should have given you this information. This court could reach ERISA itself. And then we needn't interpret ERISA at all. That's correct. We think that there is... But if we disagree with you on the contract and agree with the court below on the contract, then we must get to this question. That is correct, Your Honor. Yes. That is our view. May I ask one last question? Sure. On this subject. It's pretty difficult to amend contracts like this, or is it? Amend the trust agreement? Yes. Your Honor, the settlers of the trust, if you will, which was established in 1950-55, gave the amendment powers exclusively to the trustees. They passed the gauntlet to the trustees. And so the trustees have the right to amend the trust agreement when they think it's proved to do so in the circumstances. So it is not difficult to amend the trust agreement. But in this particular case, because of the breadth and scope of the Sixth Circuit's ruling, an amendment of the trust agreement would not get the job done here because the Sixth Circuit said, as I'll get to in a minute, if the court please, that ERISA doesn't allow you to do this the way they interpreted our contract. You can't do it. But furthermore, they add the holding that it would be arbitrary and capricious to even attempt to do an audit of this scope. Do you think they meant arbitrary and capricious under the contract as it existed, or there would have been arbitrary and capricious even if there had been an amendment to the contract that would expressly allow it? Yes, I believe the latter, Your Honor, because they indicated that they talked about the cost of auditing all of the records of allegedly non-covered employees. The decision itself would be imprudent and a waste of fund assets to even embark on such an audit. The intimation being that even if the authority were there, it would be an imprudent use of trust funds? Yes, Your Honor, very definitely. I take it that you would use accountants to do the audit, spot check? We would use and have used, Your Honor, what we call our field audit program, and it is in-house fund employees who are now trained, certified public accountants who specialize in doing audits. Why wouldn't you be satisfied with a certificate of an independent auditor employed by the employer? Well, employed by the— Everybody, every other agency in the government is satisfied with a certificate of the SEC is. Why do you need to do it yourself rather than let the employer hire an independent auditor, like some of these people who are filing amicus briefs, to do their audit and give you a certificate? Well, Your Honor, we have ultimate fiduciary responsibility under ERISA. It's a non-delegable duty. You say it's a prudent man to distrust the audit of a nationally recognized firm? Well, Your Honor, I'm not saying that the big eight accounting firms are not honorable organizations. But remember, we have over 12,000 contributing employers covering a half a million participants. Well, we might have 12,000 accountants. Well, Your Honor, they're not all Arthur Young's or Arthur Anderson's. And we have companies, a small company in Keokuk, Iowa, for example. And he may have—he might be a small—what we finally refer to as a mom-and-pop operation. And they may have 10 or 15 employees. The main answer to that question, Mr. Ludlow, is to point to the very reasons that brought ERISA into being. It was a lack of confidence in how the unions were handling these matters, was it not? Yes, Your Honor. Yes, Your Honor. But we are under ERISA 302C5 and Amex Coal totally separate from the union. And we have a fiduciary duty where the union does not. And we believe that we have the right under our trust agreement because it says the agents and representatives as designated by the trustees shall have the right to perform an on-site audit. And there's another practical question, Justice White, that I'd like to address from your question. And that's one of cost. Yes. When we—to hire a Big 8 accounting firm is fine for people that can afford it. On the other hand, my— Well, the employer could always have a choice. If it's too expensive, he'd let you come in. Well, we think, Your Honor, that as suggested by the amicus brief, I believe, in Deloitte, Haskins, and Sells, they said have Arthur Young give us a special report and objective of what they want done. And then we will do it and give the report to Arthur Young. Arthur Young, someone's going to have to pay for that. And under the trust agreement now, when we do audits of employers, the fund absorbs the cost unless there is found to be great delinquencies and points—excuse me—points where there really aren't significant audit findings. In any event, after the 260— May I ask one question, Mr. Lippo? On the question of the trustee's power to amend the trust documents, you said they had unrestricted power of amendment. I don't find that. Maybe it's not in the papers that are— It isn't, Your Honor. It was in Prasham-Schneider and its Article 10, which is the amendment powers. And it may not be in this particular case it was in Prasham-Schneider. But they can't amend the contribution obligation, can they? Oh, no. No, Your Honor. I mean, it's the contribution obligation is determined by the parties. By the collective bargaining agreement. That's correct. But the—and the coverage of what kind of employee they have to contribute on, that's also defined in the basic agreement. Yes, it is, Your Honor. And the scope of our inquiry when we do an audit— But you're saying they have the power to amend the instrument, say it was ambiguous now, to say, lest there be any doubt about it, we have the right to audit all contributing employers, including all payroll records of people not eligible to participate. They could adopt such an amendment? Yes, they have the power to do that, Your Honor, but— I don't understand why they don't, then. Well, as I tried to explain— I understand. You see, they're afraid because of what the Sixth Circuit says. The Sixth Circuit has—we are absolutely dead in the water because we believe, because of the Sixth Circuit ruling, because they not only say must you have particularized costs, that it would be imprudent. It would be arbitrary and capricious to even attempt an audit of this magnitude. And that's the key point that I wanted to stress with the Court—I see my time is flashing here—is this. The scope of our audit is a very limited inquiry. As to the allegedly non-covered employees, the employees that the employer does not admit liability to, all we want to do is establish that that employee is not doing collective bargaining agreement work. That's all we want. We don't need test scores. We don't need medical records, things that are characterized as sensitive. What we do need is, for example, we need to know, as a basic tie-in document, we need to see the 941, and we need the IRS Form 941, and the complete payroll register of an employer. Why do we need that? Because they both have to match. Because if they don't match, that means that there's possibly a ghost payroll out there somewhere, and there could be employees that are not being reported upon and reported under the collective bargaining agreement. Mr. Luplo, I take it you're not encouraging us to say that the trustees must conduct these audits. No, Your Honor. I notice you're being very careful to avoid that kind of decision. No, Your Honor, we're saying that, yes, it depends what's reasonable in the circumstances, because of our size and— Is that why you're not relying on Section 1059A1 in making your argument? Yes, Your Honor, we're saying that because of our particular plan and the scope of our operation and the multiple—the 12,000 employers and all of the people that we have sprung out over 40 states, that it is reasonable for us to do it. And besides that, we have a right under the trust agreement to do it. But I guess 1059 could be read to require employers to keep these records. Yes, Your Honor, and that would be something that—I'm not ducking the question. I know that the Solicitor General is going to ask that, but yes, I agree with that. And I see my time is up here, and I'd like to save five minutes for rebuttal, if it's all right. Mr. Schwartz. Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court. It is the view of the United States that, contrary to the decision of the Court of Appeals, both the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 and the particular trust agreements that underlie this case, authorize petitioners and trustees to confirm by prudent auditing activities that employers participating in the pension and health and welfare funds are making full contributions on behalf of all the employees for whom they are due. I would like to emphasize that the government does agree that this case could be decided exclusively on the basis of the trust agreement. We think that— Do I gather that employees are covered, even if not members of the union, if they are doing a certain kind of work which is covered by the collective bargaining agreement? That's my understanding. Even though not members of the union? Yes, I'm— I gather—and you want to be—I gather the purpose of the audit is to be sure that a lot of employees not members of the union are on covered work. Is that it? Among other things, it's one of the reasons why the alternative proposed by the respondents of looking to the union is not adequate. We think that it's a matter of law. The Court's decision is established that that wouldn't be the exclusive route anyway, but there is a good practical reason why that's correct. May I answer this question? Do the employers have separate and different retirement plans for the 60 percent of their employees who are not in the union? Respondent so states in his brief, and that's the extent of my knowledge, that they do have other plans. Yes, well, is it your contention that employees who are covered by other plans also have to be within the audit? It is our contention that in order to ascertain that all the employees who belong within a particular plan are, in fact, having contributions made for them, that a selective random sample would not exclude someone merely because the employer says, oh, they're in that plan, so they can't be in yours. It does not stand to reason that merely because the employer says that is so, and in fact may be so, that it's correct. But the major- If the employer simply proved that a particular group of employees were covered by a different plan, say a plan had been approved by ERISA. If the employer established that particular employees were in fact doing the other kind of work, then the audit would be done. Well, suppose there was a disagreement as to whether the work was other kind of work or not. If the employee were covered under another plan, is it the government's position that the trustees could audit to determine whether or not it agreed with the type of work being done? The government's position, and I think we would rely on the Schneider case from last term, that the trustees are not bound by the separate proceedings by which two unions and an employer might resolve their disputes as to coverage. The trustees have a right to determine, and the focus is very factual, what kind of work is being done. That is not to say that there is no role for deference to the other kinds of proceedings that resolve the question of which work belongs in which plan. But the employee, the trustees still have a right to find out the facts of what kind of work an individual is doing. It's whatever it might be. The procedure, however, it's done. Suppose it's found that given work is covered under this agreement, but it's being done by non-members of the union, and the employer has provided a pension fund for those. Now, may there be an audit, and if it's discovered that the work they're doing, in fact, even though there's a pension fund for them, that the work they're doing is covered by the collective bargaining agreement, then they must be included? I believe this point is actually addressed in the reply brief of the petitioners and is not in our own brief, but it's my understanding that if, in fact, you are covered, then contributions are due to be made. And it's also my understanding, although largely based on petitioners' argument in that reply brief, that there are procedures available to see that the employee never comes up short and also that the employer need not make two sets of payments. The government hasn't taken a position on the question he asked you. No, I don't think so. The audit authority would extend to those people. So the audit authority would include people covered by another plan when obviously they wouldn't have been included under it if it had not been thought they were doing work outside of the union. But the question is whether that whoever thought that thought so correctly. So you audit all 100 percent of the employees. You don't audit 100 percent. You audit selectively, but you need not exclude someone chosen at random simply because the employer tells you. Who decides how many you audit? Well, I think that's a question of prudent professional auditing judgment. Just as we're not arguing that you must do an audit in every case, accountants and auditors have professional standards as to what is a sufficient sampling, a very small number, we're clear, to provide assurance. And if you try a few and you get discrepancies and you look at more, if you try a few and you don't get discrepancies, you don't look at more. Auditors competent to determine whether or not the work being done comes within a particular plan or not, under a particular union agreement or not? Justice Powell, we think that generally there's not a problem here because contrary to what respondents suggest, this is basically a problem of jurisdictional dispute. Our understanding is that the problem is essentially omissions. People who drop out of sight, particularly in certain industries where employment is seasonal, variable, or temporary, or there's a lot of shifting between employers, the Secretary of Labor has reason to believe that a lot of people just drop out of the system and that there are omissions and that therefore it is unrealistic to think of this as a backdoor form of jurisdictional warfare among unions. You really think the auditors are better equipped to do that than the union itself? Yes, because it's precisely in those situations where the union may well not know who is there. But the auditors would know better about the type of work? If the – I'm trying to communicate the idea that these are relatively simple, factual determinations. If you pick out a file and the employment application shows 20 years of truck driving and three merit awards for safe driving and the employer claims that this person is in the bookkeeper's union, I think an auditor would be qualified to say that this is a suspect determination and to inquire further on the basis of that. And I don't think that the kind of – and it is those kind of factual things that the auditors are looking for and that they are reasonably qualified to engage in it. And then, of course, the fund trustees sit down with the employers and work out the initially determined discrepancies. And the employer, of course, has the opportunity to say, well, there really is an explanation for this. Mr. Horst, a while ago, before you were questioned, you end up saying that – did you say that you do not agree that the case could be decided on the collective bargaining agreement? No, quite the reverse, Justice White. We do believe that it could be decided that way. Only if we agree with you on what the collective bargaining agreement means. On what the trust agreements mean. On the trust, yes. Yeah, I should also point out there's a kind of – But if we disagree with that, if we agree with the court below that the trust agreement does not provide for this audit, then you must get to the statute. That's right. Because the statute does rather clearly, in the language that you read, say, except we're inconsistent. And the legislative history of that language – Well, do you – do you – do you – is part of your submission that the contract, that the trust agreement does provide for the audit? Yes. Or are you taking a position? We take the position in the last section of our brief that it does quite clearly provide for it. In fact, that was the basis of our suggestion when the court initially asked for the government's views on the case, that the case should be simply sent back in light of language. In the Schneider case, which we thought read this same trust agreement the same way that we do – If we didn't agree – if we didn't agree with you on the contract, do you agree with your colleague on your side that the employer could not satisfy his ERISA obligations by having an independent auditor give a certificate with respect to all of his employees? As I read the statute and I look to Section 1020 – Section 1023A3A, the statute requires that an – that the plan trustees, when filing their annual report with a secretary, have their own independent auditor look at – assess and test the books of the – of the plan and make such tests as are required by internally accepted accounting standards. Well, here's a national firm that comes in to be a lawyer and gives a certificate in it, goes through the same procedures that the trustees would. And it would not be – you think the statute requires the trustees to reject that certificate? And do one that's of its own? It's – It doesn't sound very sensible. It's not clear to me that it would always – if I may answer – it's not clear to me that it would always be prudent to do that. The statute seems to place the burden on the trustees. There are a few reasons why I think that solution is not an adequate answer to the case. The first is I do not read respondents as accepting that solution, although the Court, of course, could differ. Well, that is what I ask you. The second is there is the problem of cost, and the Court of Appeals and respondents were very concerned about the cost of – of these procedures. And it's reasonably clear to me that the cost would be greater were the trust fund to have to bear the cost of retaining respondents' independent auditor to do this audit. It's also not at all clear to me, as I read Deloitte's – Haskins' – Sells' brief – that this offer of comedy, essentially, is – among auditors – is one that is available to anyone other than the independent auditor, which is Arthur Young and not Mr. Luplo's client. Time is expired now, Mr. Schwartz. Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice. Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice. Mr. Moran. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court. The question before the Court today is by what authority do these trustees, these Taft-Harley funds, find the power to investigate records of employees that the union and the employer have together determined are not doing collective bargaining unit work? Mr. Mr. President, does the public have any way of knowing whether the union and the employer hadn't, by tacit agreement, decided to do these people in and not comply with the provisions of the trust or the statute? I'd like to answer that question in two parts, if I may, Mr. Chief Justice. Mr. President, I'd like to ask you, Mr. President, to be sure that the employers remit all funds that are necessary in the form of compensation and payment of fringe benefits. Mr. President, some of these unions have been notable for some other factors in connection with trust funds, too, have they not? I don't follow the question, Your Honor. Well, corruption in the trust funds. The corruption in the trust funds of these funds, Your Honor, has been the subject of some litigation launched by the Department of Labor in the Northern District of Illinois Federal Court. And as a result of allegations of gross mismanagement, these very funds have given, by consent judgment, their investment management funds, or powers, rather, to an independent investment manager. I'm not aware of any allegations that deal with our client or with the Teamsters union or locals with which we deal of any misuse of funds by that union. I'm not addressing the particular unions. I'm talking about the thrust and purpose of this whole program in the minds of Congress. What were they trying to do? Congress was trying, in passing, ERISA, Your Honor, to make sure that if an employer gives fringe benefit funds to his employees, that all employees would be eligible to participate in that fund. But Congress did not say to the employers that if you, employer, have more than one fund, each of your employees must be a participant in each of your funds. Not at all. Congress allowed certain discriminations, certain characteristics of employment, that would allow one employee to be a member of one pension fund, and another employee of the same employer to be a member of a different pension fund. The complement of employees that Central Transport has is made up of three broad categories. The first are those who are members of the Teamsters union, who operate within the jurisdiction of the Central States fund, and are participants in that fund. The second are members of the Teamsters union that operate in a different geographic area of the country, and are participants in a different Taft-Hartley fund. Also, within that second group, are members of other unions, like the International Association of Machinists, which have a separate Taft-Hartley plan. And finally, there are those employees who are not members of any union, who can qualify, if they meet the definition of ERISA participant, to be a participant in the employer-sponsored pension fund that is maintained by Central Transport. Justice O'Connor asked a question earlier, followed up by Mr. Justice Brennan. Must a person be a member of the union to be a participant in these funds? And I think the answer was given that, no, these funds represent a broad spectrum of participants, and not all participants have to be members of the union. But that's not the facts in this case. Central Transport is a closed shop. To do bargaining unit work in Central Transport, you must be a member of the Teamsters union within 30 days. That's covered quite clearly in the collective bargaining agreement. That's the deal. It is true under ERISA generally that you could have people who were not union members, but nevertheless employees participating in a plan. In a plan. That is absolutely correct. Right. And for that reason, as we interpret ERISA, it's logical that we couldn't rely on the union's efforts to see to it that contributions are made for everyone, because the union wouldn't have a lot of interest in someone who wasn't a union member, presumably. And yet the fund and the safety of the fund's investments to cover potential eventual retirements would depend on collecting for everyone who's, in fact, a participant. The question or the comment, if I may, Your Honor, points out a difficulty in this court attempting to make a broad sweep of authority to Taft-Hartley trustees in general. In the case at bar, to be a participant in the central states fund, the employee of Central Transport must be a member of the union. Is that true of every single employer who's covered by this collective bargaining agreement? I am told by the funds that that is not true because they operate in right-to-work states. Well, then, you're just representing one company, aren't you? That's it. I am representing a group of 16 companies that all operate in the same geographic area. And that group, all are closed shops? Absolutely. But that is not true of a lot of the other participants or companies that contribute to the fund? I am told that that is not true by the petitioners, Your Honor. But nevertheless, your case, the only things before us are 16 closed shop companies. That is correct. But in interpreting ERISA, if we get that far in this case, we would have to be careful about our rationale and view of the fact that it might include employees who aren't union members. Isn't that so? That's absolutely correct, Justice O'Connor. And that's the very reason that this Court should not embark upon attempting to find implied in ERISA that which is not there. If Congress wished to give a power to the trustees, Congress knows how to express its purpose. Section 1104 of Code of Title 29, which sets forth the duties and obligations of these trustees, has no mention of the power to audit non-participants. Why do you suppose Section 1059 requires the employer to maintain records for all employees, not only planned participants? Because, Justice O'Connor, 1059 is dealing with the ERISA definition of employee, which is found at 1002, parent 6. It deals with a requirement that the employer maintain records. And that indicates to me maybe a broader concern than you are expressing. If I may, Your Honor, within the definition of employee, as stated by ERISA, are several components. The employees of Central Transport who can qualify for participation in this plan are only one portion of that total component of employee definition. And we agree full well that the definition of employee in ERISA is much broader than the definition of employee in the collective bargaining agreement. And therein lies our controversy. Mr. Ram, I'm getting a little confused. These are all closed shops, all 16 of the companies you represent today? That's correct, Your Honor. Well, surely the trustees may audit the records of all of those employees, may it not? The trustees may audit the records of all employees who are members of the union and are doing bargaining unit work. Yes. Well, then what other employees are there? If I may. Yes. Central Transport has a number of different employee groups. Some of them are Teamsters. And some of those Teamsters operate in the geographic area represented by these funds. Some of them are Teamsters and do not operate in the geographic area represented by these funds. Just taking those two components, these trustees clearly have the right to review the records of Teamsters who are operating within their geographic area. And they have done so, and they did so for 60 days.
